newsitem.title: USA: Conn. comptroller sees bigger FY 1997 surplus.
newsitem.headline: Conn. comptroller sees bigger FY 1997 surplus.

text.p: The Connecticut Comptroller on Wednesday said that the state would get an even bigger surplus than she estimated earlier because the state's economy improved while financial markets were firm.

Nancy Wyman, in a letter to Gov. John Rowland that was released by her office, projected the state would collect an extra $184 million, $64 million higher than the forecast she made several months ago.

Wyman said Rowland only was counting the surplus as $11.9 million because he wanted to use it for spending that normally would be included in the 1998 fiscal year that starts on July 1--a practice upon which she frowned.

"I continue to be concerned that your planned use of this year's one-time surplus to advance permanent changes in the state's revenue base will create long-term strucutural state deficits," Wyman said.
And she criticized Rowland for not putting the surplus in the state's Rainy Day Fund, a short-term stabilization fund that can be drawn upon during an economic downturn.

Connecticut's general fund spending for fiscal 1997 was estimated at $188.2 million above the amount appropriated by the legislature. The biggest excess spending was seen in Medicaid, at $44.1 million over budget, and foster care for children, at $35.5 million over. But income tax receipts were expected to top the budget by $199 million, and sales taxes were projected at $8.1 million over, according to Wyman.

Along with the House Speaker, Tom Ritter, Wyman has urged legislators not to accept Rowland's proposal to drop the state's move to Generally Accepted Accounting Practices, which at present state law requires, starting July 1.
